questions.solution: The two acute angles of a right triangle add to $90^\circ$ (since the right angle uses 90 of the 180). If the smaller is $x$, then $x + 4x = 90$, so $5x = 90$ and $x = 18$.

solve.work: Acute angles sum to 90: x + 4x = 90 -> x = 18. Angles 18 and 72.

questions.skill: Tell which information fixes exactly one triangle
questions.stem: Which information is enough to build exactly one triangle, so that every triangle that fits it has the same size and shape?
choices: Side lengths of 4 cm, 6 cm and 9 cm
Two side lengths, 5 cm and 7 cm
One side of 6 cm and one angle of $50^\circ$
questions.answer: Side lengths of 4 cm, 6 cm and 9 cm
questions.solution: Three side lengths that satisfy the triangle condition ($4 + 6 > 9$) give one triangle. Three angles fix only the shape, so triangles of any size fit. Two sides, or one side and one angle, leave other measures free.

solve.answer: Side lengths of 4 cm, 6 cm and 9 cm
solve.work: One side and one angle: many triangles. Two sides alone: many. Three angles: same shape, any size. Three sides 4, 6, 9 (4+6=10>9, valid): exactly one triangle (SSS).

questions.skill: Side lengths: can they form a triangle?
questions.stem: Which set of lengths, in meters, can be the sides of a triangle?
questions.solution: $2.5 + 3 = 5.5 > 5$, so 2.5, 3, 5 works. In 1.5, 2, 4 the short sides add to 3.5. In 3, 3, 6.5 they add to 6. In 0.8, 1.1, 2.2 they add to 1.9. Each of those is less than the longest side.

questions.skill: Side lengths: can they form a triangle?
questions.stem: Four sets of whole-number side lengths are tested: 7, 10, 18; 12, 13, 26; 9, 9, 18; 5, 11, 15. How many of the sets can form a triangle?
questions.solution: 7, 10, 18: $17 < 18$ fails. 12, 13, 26: $25 < 26$ fails. 9, 9, 18: $18$ is not more than 18, fails. 5, 11, 15: $5 + 11 = 16 > 15$ works. Only one set works.

questions.skill: Side lengths: can they form a triangle?
questions.stem: Which set of lengths, in feet, can NOT be the sides of a triangle?
questions.solution: For $\frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{3}{4}$: $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{4}$, which is not MORE than $\frac{3}{4}$, so no triangle. The other three sets each have two short sides that add to more than the longest: $\frac{7}{6} > \frac{3}{4}$, $\frac{5}{6} > \frac{2}{3}$ and $\frac{5}{4} > \frac{3}{4}$.

questions.skill: Side lengths: can they form a triangle?
questions.stem: Ana has sticks that are 4, 5, 9 and 11 centimeters long. She picks three of the four sticks. How many different groups of three sticks can she join into a triangle?
questions.solution: The groups are: 4, 5, 9 ($9$ is not more than 9, fails); 4, 5, 11 ($9 < 11$, fails); 4, 9, 11 ($13 > 11$, works); 5, 9, 11 ($14 > 11$, works). Two groups work.

questions.skill: Side lengths: can they form a triangle?
questions.stem: Set P has side lengths 7, 8 and 15. Set Q has side lengths 7, 8 and 14. Which statement is true?
choices: Only set P can be the sides of a triangle
Only set Q can be the sides of a triangle
Both sets can be the sides of a triangle
Neither set can be the sides of a triangle
questions.answer: Only set Q can be the sides of a triangle
questions.solution: Set P: $7 + 8 = 15$, which is not more than 15, so P is not a triangle. Set Q: $7 + 8 = 15 > 14$, so Q is a triangle.

solve.answer: Only set Q can be the sides of a triangle
solve.work: P: 7+8=15, equal to 15, not greater: no triangle. Q: 7+8=15>14: triangle. Only set Q.

questions.skill: Range of the third side
questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle are 8 inches and 3 inches. The third side is a whole number of inches. What is the shortest length it can have, in inches?
questions.solution: The third side must be more than $8 - 3 = 5$. The least whole number more than 5 is 6. Check: $3 + 6 = 9 > 8$.

solve.work: Third side > 8-3 = 5 and < 11. Shortest whole number is 6 (3+6=9>8).

questions.skill: Range of the third side
questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle are 6 cm and 10 cm. The third side is $x$ cm. Which describes every possible value of $x$?
questions.solution: $x$ must be less than $6 + 10 = 16$ and more than $10 - 6 = 4$, with neither end allowed (those would lie flat). So $4 < x < 16$.

solve.work: Need x < 6+10 = 16 and x > 10-6 = 4, strictly (equality gives a flat figure). So 4 < x < 16.

questions.skill: Range of the third side
questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle are 7 cm and 12 cm. The third side is a whole number of centimeters. What is the greatest possible perimeter of the triangle, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The third side must be less than $7 + 12 = 19$, so at most 18. The greatest perimeter is $7 + 12 + 18 = 37$ centimeters.

solve.work: Third side < 7+12 = 19, so at most 18 (and 18 > 5). Greatest perimeter 7+12+18 = 37.

questions.skill: Range of the third side
questions.stem: A triangle has sides of 15 cm and 6 cm. Which could be the length of the third side, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The third side must be more than $15 - 6 = 9$ and less than $15 + 6 = 21$. Only 12 is between 9 and 21. A 9 cm side gives $6 + 9 = 15$ and a 21 cm side gives $15 + 6 = 21$: both lie flat.

solve.work: Third side between 15-6=9 and 15+6=21, strictly. 8 too short, 9 and 21 flat. 12 works.

questions.skill: Range of the third side
questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle are 4 cm and 8 cm. The third side could be 2, 5, 9 or 13 cm long. How many of these four lengths could really be the third side?
questions.solution: The third side must be more than $8 - 4 = 4$ and less than $4 + 8 = 12$. Of 2, 5, 9 and 13, only 5 and 9 are between 4 and 12. So 2 of the lengths work.

solve.work: Third side must be between 8-4=4 and 8+4=12. 2 no, 5 yes, 9 yes, 13 no. Two lengths.

questions.skill: Isosceles triangles and the side condition
questions.stem: An isosceles triangle has one side of 3 cm and one side of 7 cm. What is its perimeter, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The third side equals one of the two. If it were 3, the sides 3, 3, 7 would fail, since $3 + 3 = 6 < 7$. So the third side is 7, and the sides are 7, 7, 3. The perimeter is $7 + 7 + 3 = 17$ centimeters.

questions.skill: Isosceles triangles and the side condition
questions.stem: Which set of side lengths, in centimeters, can be the sides of an isosceles triangle?
questions.solution: $6 + 6 = 12 > 11$, so 6, 6, 11 works. For 3, 3, 6 the sum is exactly 6. For 5, 5, 11 it is 10 and for 4, 4, 9 it is 8: both less than the third side.

questions.skill: Isosceles triangles and the side condition
questions.stem: An isosceles triangle has a base of 4 cm. Its two equal sides are each a whole number of centimeters. What is the shortest each of the equal sides can be, in centimeters?
questions.solution: Two equal sides must add to more than the base: they must be more than $4 \div 2 = 2$ each. The least whole number more than 2 is 3. Check: $3 + 3 = 6 > 4$.

solve.work: Equal sides s with base 4: need s+s > 4, so s > 2. Shortest whole number s = 3 (3,3,4: 6>4).

questions.skill: Missing angle from the 180 degree sum
questions.stem: A triangle has an angle of $120^\circ$ and an angle of $25^\circ$. What is the measure of the third angle, in degrees?

questions.skill: Missing angle from the 180 degree sum
questions.stem: An isosceles triangle has a top angle of $40^\circ$ between its two equal sides. What is the measure of one of the other two angles, in degrees?
questions.solution: The other two angles are equal and share $180 - 40 = 140$ degrees, so each is $140 \div 2 = 70$ degrees. The number 140 forgets to split between the two angles.

solve.work: The other two angles are equal: (180 - 40)/2 = 70.

questions.skill: Missing angle from the 180 degree sum
questions.stem: In a right triangle, one acute angle measures $37^\circ$. What is the measure of the other acute angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The right angle is $90^\circ$, so the two acute angles share $180 - 90 = 90$ degrees. The other is $90 - 37 = 53$ degrees.

solve.work: Acute angles of a right triangle sum to 90: 90 - 37 = 53.

questions.skill: Angle sum with algebra or ratios
questions.stem: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio $3:4:5$. What is the measure of the smallest angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: There are $3 + 4 + 5 = 12$ equal parts in $180^\circ$, so one part is $180 \div 12 = 15$ degrees. The smallest angle is $3 \times 15 = 45$ degrees.

questions.skill: Angle sum with algebra or ratios
questions.stem: The angles of a triangle measure $(x+20)^\circ$, $(x+30)^\circ$ and $(x+40)^\circ$. Which equation can be used to find $x$?
questions.solution: The three angles of a triangle ADD to $180^\circ$, so $(x+20)+(x+30)+(x+40)=180$. The second equation uses the wrong total, the third forgets that $x$ is in every angle, and the fourth multiplies instead of adding.

solve.work: Angle sum of a triangle is 180, so (x+20)+(x+30)+(x+40)=180. The 360 option uses the wrong total, the product is wrong, and x+20+30+40 drops two x's.

questions.skill: Angle sum with algebra or ratios
questions.stem: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio $1:1:4$. What is the measure of the largest angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: There are $1 + 1 + 4 = 6$ parts, so one part is $180 \div 6 = 30$ degrees. The largest angle is $4 \times 30 = 120$ degrees.

questions.skill: Which angle measures can form a triangle
questions.stem: Which set of angle measures, in degrees, can NOT be the angles of a triangle?
questions.solution: $100 + 45 + 45 = 190$, which is more than 180, so these cannot be the angles of a triangle. The other sets add to 180.

questions.skill: Which angle measures can form a triangle
questions.stem: Dan measures the three angles of a paper triangle and gets $71^\circ$, $54^\circ$ and $63^\circ$. The angles of a triangle should add to $180^\circ$. By how many degrees is Dan's total off?

questions.skill: Which angle measures can form a triangle
questions.stem: Which statement about the angles of a triangle is true?
choices: A triangle can have two right angles
A triangle can have one obtuse angle and two acute angles
A triangle can have two obtuse angles
A triangle can have one right angle and one obtuse angle
questions.answer: A triangle can have one obtuse angle and two acute angles
questions.solution: An obtuse angle is more than $90^\circ$ and a right angle is exactly $90^\circ$. Two angles of these kinds would already add to more than $180^\circ$ with the third angle still to come. One obtuse angle with two acute angles is possible, for example $100^\circ$, $40^\circ$ and $40^\circ$.

solve.answer: A triangle can have one obtuse angle and two acute angles
solve.work: Two obtuse or two right angles, or right+obtuse, already reach 180 or more, leaving nothing for a third angle. One obtuse with two acute (e.g. 100, 40, 40) works.

questions.skill: How many triangles fit the given measures
questions.stem: A triangle has angles of $40^\circ$ and $60^\circ$, and the side between those two angles is 7 cm long. How many different triangles fit this description?
questions.solution: Two angles and the side between them fix the triangle: the third angle is $80^\circ$ and the rest follows. There is exactly 1 triangle.

solve.work: Two angles and the included side (ASA) fix the triangle; 40+60 < 180. Exactly one.

questions.skill: How many triangles fit the given measures
questions.stem: Priya wants two classmates to build exactly the same triangle from her instructions. Which instructions should she give?
choices: Two sides of 5 cm and 7 cm, and the $60^\circ$ angle between them
One side of 8 cm and one angle of $40^\circ$
questions.answer: Two sides of 5 cm and 7 cm, and the $60^\circ$ angle between them
questions.solution: Two sides and the angle between them leave only one way to close the triangle. Two angles, or one side and one angle, leave sizes or shapes free, and three angles allow triangles of many sizes.

solve.answer: Two sides of 5 cm and 7 cm, and the $60^\circ$ angle between them
solve.work: Two sides and the included angle (SAS) fix one triangle. Three angles or two angles give many sizes; one side and one angle give many.

questions.skill: How many triangles fit the given measures
questions.stem: A triangle has angles of $50^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. A side of 9 cm is opposite the $50^\circ$ angle. How many different triangles fit this description?
questions.solution: The third angle is $180 - 50 - 60 = 70$ degrees. Two angles and a side fix the triangle, and 9 cm opposite the $50^\circ$ angle sets the size. There is exactly 1 triangle.

solve.work: Third angle 70. Angles fixed and the side opposite 50 is 9 cm: AAS fixes one triangle (scale is set by that side).

questions.skill: How many triangles fit the given measures
questions.stem: Four sets of directions for drawing a triangle are given. Which set leads to no triangle at all?
choices: Sides of 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm
Sides of 3 cm, 3 cm and 8 cm
Angles of $40^\circ$ and $70^\circ$ with a 5 cm side between them
questions.answer: Sides of 3 cm, 3 cm and 8 cm
questions.solution: $3 + 3 = 6 < 8$, so those sides cannot make a triangle. The sides 4, 5, 6 work ($9 > 6$), the angles $20 + 60 + 100 = 180$ work, and two angles with the side between them always work when they add to less than $180^\circ$.

solve.answer: Sides of 3 cm, 3 cm and 8 cm
solve.work: 3+3 = 6 < 8: no triangle. 20+60+100 = 180 works; 4,5,6 works; 40+70 < 180 with included side works. Answer: sides 3, 3, 8.

questions.skill: Reason with a model, a rule or a claim
questions.stem: Ana says, "The sticks of 7 cm, 9 cm and 16 cm will make a triangle, because 7 + 9 is greater than 16." Which statement about Ana is correct?
choices: Ana is wrong, because 7 + 9 equals 16 and is not greater than 16
Ana is right, because 16 is the longest side
Ana is right, because all three lengths are different
Ana is wrong, because 7 + 16 is less than 9
questions.answer: Ana is wrong, because 7 + 9 equals 16 and is not greater than 16
questions.solution: $7 + 9 = 16$, which is equal to 16, not greater. The sticks would lie flat, so there is no triangle. Ana is wrong, and her reason fails because of that.

solve.answer: Ana is wrong, because 7 + 9 equals 16 and is not greater than 16
solve.work: 7 + 9 = 16, equal to the longest stick, not greater; Ana's claim '7 + 9 is greater than 16' is false and no triangle forms.

questions.skill: Reason with a model, a rule or a claim
questions.stem: Two students each build a triangle from sticks of 6 cm, 7 cm and 8 cm. What is true about their triangles?
choices: They can have different angles, as a four-stick frame can lean
They must be the same size and shape, because three side lengths fix a triangle
They can have different angles, depending on which stick is laid at the bottom
They can be the same size but not the same shape
questions.answer: They must be the same size and shape, because three side lengths fix a triangle
questions.solution: A triangle made from three given sticks is rigid: it cannot lean or change its angles. Any two such triangles are exactly the same size and shape (one may just be turned or flipped over).

solve.answer: They must be the same size and shape, because three side lengths fix a triangle
solve.work: Three side lengths determine a unique triangle (SSS): both triangles are congruent, same size and shape, whichever side is at the bottom.

questions.skill: Reason with a model, a rule or a claim
questions.stem: Which statement is true?
choices: Any two obtuse angles can be two of the angles of a triangle
Any two right angles can be two of the angles of a triangle
Any two acute angles can be two of the angles of a triangle
Any two angles can be two of the angles of a triangle
questions.answer: Any two acute angles can be two of the angles of a triangle
questions.solution: Each acute angle is less than $90^\circ$, so two acute angles add to less than $180^\circ$ and a third angle is left over. Two obtuse angles, or two right angles, already add to $180^\circ$ or more.

solve.answer: Any two acute angles can be two of the angles of a triangle
solve.work: Two acute angles sum to less than 180, leaving a positive third angle, so it always works. Two right or two obtuse angles reach 180 or more; 'any two angles' fails for e.g. 100 and 100.

questions.skill: Reason with a model, a rule or a claim
questions.stem: Two sticks, 5 cm and 8 cm long, are joined at one end by a hinge. A string connects their free ends to make the third side of a triangle. The hinge can open to any angle between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, but not to exactly $0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$. The string is a whole number of centimeters long. What is the longest string that can still make a triangle, in centimeters?
questions.solution: When the hinge is almost flat (nearly $180^\circ$), the string is nearly $5 + 8 = 13$ cm, but it must be less than 13 cm. The greatest whole number is 12 centimeters.

solve.work: Hinge angle strictly between 0 and 180 means the string is strictly between 8-5 = 3 and 8+5 = 13. Longest whole number 12.

questions.skill: Count the possible whole-number lengths of a third side
questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle are 8 cm and 11 cm long. The third side is a whole number of centimeters. How many different lengths are possible for the third side?
questions.solution: The third side must be greater than $11 - 8 = 3$ and less than $8 + 11 = 19$. The whole numbers from 4 to 18 work, and there are $18 - 4 + 1 = 15$ of them.

questions.skill: Use an algebra equation with the angle sum of a triangle
questions.stem: The angles of a triangle measure $x$ degrees, $(2x + 10)$ degrees and $(3x - 10)$ degrees. What is the measure of the largest angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The angles add to 180: $x + (2x + 10) + (3x - 10) = 6x = 180$, so $x = 30$. The angles are $30$, $2(30) + 10 = 70$ and $3(30) - 10 = 80$. The largest is 80 degrees.

questions.skill: Decide how many triangles fit given sides and the angle between them
questions.stem: A triangle has one side of 10 cm and another side of 12 cm, and the angle between those two sides is $30^\circ$. How many triangles with different shapes or sizes can be built with these measurements?
questions.answer: Exactly one
questions.solution: Two sides and the angle between them fix the third side and the other two angles, so only one triangle (up to identical size and shape) can be built.

solve.answer: Exactly one
solve.work: Two sides and the included angle (SAS) fix the triangle: exactly one.

questions.skill: Side lengths: can they form a triangle?
questions.stem: Five sets of side lengths, in centimeters, are listed: 1.2, 1.5, 2.8; 2.4, 3.1, 5.4; 0.9, 0.9, 1.9; 4.5, 5, 9.4; 3.2, 3.2, 6.4. How many of the sets can be the sides of a triangle?

questions.skill: Side lengths: can they form a triangle?
questions.stem: Five sticks are 2, 4, 5, 8 and 9 centimeters long. Three of the sticks are chosen and joined end to end. How many different groups of three sticks can make a triangle?
questions.solution: There are 10 groups. Working: 2, 4, 5 works ($6 > 5$); 2, 4, 8 and 2, 4, 9 fail; 2, 5, 8 and 2, 5, 9 fail; 2, 8, 9 works ($10 > 9$); 4, 5, 8 works ($9 > 8$); 4, 5, 9 fails ($9$ is not more than 9); 4, 8, 9 works; 5, 8, 9 works. That is 5 groups.

questions.skill: Side lengths: can they form a triangle?
questions.stem: These sets of side lengths are in centimeters. Set A: 10, 14, 25. Set B: 10, 14, 24. Set C: 10, 14, 23. Which sets can be the sides of a triangle?
questions.answer: Only set C
questions.solution: The two shorter sides in each set are 10 and 14, which add to 24. Set A needs 24 to be more than 25: no. Set B needs 24 to be more than 24: no. Set C needs 24 to be more than 23: yes.

solve.answer: Only set C

questions.skill: Side lengths: can they form a triangle?
questions.stem: Three sticks have lengths that are three consecutive whole numbers of centimeters, such as 5, 6 and 7. The sticks can be joined into a triangle. What is the smallest possible total length of the three sticks, in centimeters?
questions.solution: Try the smallest sets. 1, 2, 3: $1 + 2 = 3$, not more than 3, so it is flat. 2, 3, 4: $2 + 3 = 5 > 4$, so it works. The total is $2 + 3 + 4 = 9$ centimeters.

solve.work: Sides n, n+1, n+2 need n+(n+1)>n+2, so n>1. 1,2,3: 3=3 fails. 2,3,4: 5>4 works. Smallest total 2+3+4=9.

questions.skill: Range of the third side
questions.stem: A sailmaker is cutting a triangular sail. Two of its edges are 9 meters and 14 meters long. The third edge is a whole number of meters. How many different lengths could the third edge have?
questions.solution: The third edge is more than $14 - 9 = 5$ and less than $9 + 14 = 23$. The whole numbers from 6 to 22 are possible: $22 - 6 + 1 = 17$ lengths.

solve.work: Third edge between 14-9=5 and 14+9=23, strictly: whole numbers 6 to 22, that is 22-6+1 = 17 lengths.

questions.skill: Range of the third side
questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle are 4 cm and 11 cm long. The third side is a whole number of centimeters. What is the least possible perimeter of the triangle, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The third side must be more than $11 - 4 = 7$, so at least 8. The least perimeter is $4 + 11 + 8 = 23$ centimeters.

solve.work: Third side > 11-4 = 7, so at least 8. Least perimeter 4+11+8 = 23.

questions.skill: Range of the third side
questions.stem: Towns A, B and C are not on one straight line. Town B is 14 km from town A and 6 km from town C. The distance from A to C is a whole number of kilometers. What is the shortest it can be, in kilometers?
questions.solution: A, B and C form a triangle with sides 14 and 6, so the third side AC is more than $14 - 6 = 8$. The least whole number more than 8 is 9.

solve.work: Not on one line, so A, B, C form a triangle with AB=14, BC=6. AC > 14-6 = 8 (and < 20). Shortest whole number is 9.

questions.skill: Range of the third side
questions.stem: A triangle has sides of 8 cm and 13 cm, and a third side that is a whole number of centimeters. Which lists the smallest and largest whole-number lengths the third side can have?
questions.answer: Smallest 6, largest 20
questions.solution: The third side is more than $13 - 8 = 5$, so at least 6. It is less than $8 + 13 = 21$, so at most 20.

solve.answer: Smallest 6, largest 20
solve.work: Third side between 13-8=5 and 13+8=21, strictly. Whole numbers 6 to 20. Smallest 6, largest 20.

questions.skill: Range of the third side
questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle are 3 cm and 5 cm. The third side is a whole number of centimeters. What is the sum of all the possible lengths of the third side, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The third side is more than $5 - 3 = 2$ and less than $3 + 5 = 8$. The possible lengths are 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, and $3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 = 25$.

solve.work: Third side between 5-3=2 and 5+3=8, strictly: 3,4,5,6,7. Sum 3+4+5+6+7 = 25.

questions.skill: Isosceles triangles and the side condition
questions.stem: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 29 cm. One of its sides is 5 cm long. What is the length of each of the two equal sides, in centimeters?
questions.solution: If 5 cm were one of the equal sides, the sides would be 5, 5 and 19, but $5 + 5 = 10 < 19$ fails. So 5 cm is the odd side, and the two equal sides share the rest: $(29 - 5) \div 2 = 12$ centimeters. Check: $5 + 12 > 12$.

solve.work: If 5 were an equal side: 5,5,19, and 10<19 fails. So 5 is the base: equal sides (29-5)/2 = 12; 12,12,5 works. Answer 12.

questions.skill: Isosceles triangles and the side condition
questions.stem: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 20 cm and whole-number side lengths. Which of these can NOT be the length of one of its two equal sides, in centimeters?
questions.solution: If the equal sides are $a$, the third side is $20 - 2a$. For $a = 5$ the sides are 5, 5, 10, which lie flat. For $a = 6$: 6, 6, 8 works. For $a = 7$: 7, 7, 6 works. For $a = 8$: 8, 8, 4 works.

solve.work: Equal sides e, base 20-2e. 7: 7,7,6 ok. 5: 5,5,10, 5+5=10 not >10, fails. 6: 6,6,8 ok. 8: 8,8,4 ok. Cannot be 5.

questions.skill: Isosceles triangles and the side condition
questions.stem: How many different isosceles triangles with whole-number side lengths in centimeters have a perimeter of 22 cm? Triangles with the same three side lengths count as one.
questions.solution: If the equal sides are $a$, the base is $22 - 2a$, and the base must be less than $2a$, so $a$ is at least 6; the base must be positive, so $a$ is at most 10. The triangles are 6, 6, 10; 7, 7, 8; 8, 8, 6; 9, 9, 4; 10, 10, 2. That is 5 triangles.

solve.work: Equal sides e, base 22-2e > 0 so e <= 10; need 2e > 22-2e so e > 5.5, e >= 6. e = 6,7,8,9,10 gives 6,6,10; 7,7,8; 8,8,6; 9,9,4; 10,10,2. No equilateral (22 not divisible by 3), so no double counting. Five.

questions.skill: Missing angle from the 180 degree sum
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, angle $A$ measures $47^\circ$. Angle $B$ is $13^\circ$ larger than angle $A$. What is the measure of angle $C$, in degrees?
questions.solution: Angle $B$ is $47 + 13 = 60$ degrees. Then angle $C$ is $180 - 47 - 60 = 73$ degrees.

questions.skill: Missing angle from the 180 degree sum
questions.stem: Two angles of a triangle measure $38^\circ$ and $52^\circ$. Which kind of triangle is it?
questions.answer: It is a right triangle
questions.solution: $38 + 52 = 90$, so the third angle is $180 - 90 = 90$ degrees. A triangle with a $90^\circ$ angle is a right triangle.

solve.answer: It is a right triangle
solve.work: Third angle = 180 - 38 - 52 = 90. It has a right angle: right triangle.

questions.skill: Angle sum with algebra or ratios
questions.stem: The angles of a triangle measure $(3x-5)^\circ$, $(2x+15)^\circ$ and $(x+20)^\circ$. What is the measure of the largest angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: $(3x-5)+(2x+15)+(x+20)=6x+30=180$, so $6x=150$ and $x=25$. The angles are $70^\circ$, $65^\circ$ and $45^\circ$, so the largest is 70 degrees.

questions.skill: Angle sum with algebra or ratios
questions.stem: In a triangle, one angle is 4 times the smallest angle, and the third angle is $30^\circ$ larger than the smallest angle. What is the measure of the largest angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: Let the smallest angle be $s$. Then $s + 4s + (s+30) = 180$, so $6s = 150$ and $s = 25$. The angles are 25, 100 and 55 degrees, so the largest is 100 degrees.

solve.work: Smallest s; others 4s and s+30. 6s+30 = 180, s = 25. Angles 25, 100, 55; 25 is indeed smallest. Largest 100.

questions.skill: Angle sum with algebra or ratios
questions.stem: In a triangle, the largest angle is 3 times the smallest angle, and the middle angle is $20^\circ$ larger than the smallest angle. What is the measure of the middle angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: Let the smallest angle be $s$. Then $s + (s+20) + 3s = 180$, so $5s = 160$ and $s = 32$. The middle angle is $32 + 20 = 52$ degrees. (The angles are 32, 52 and 96.)

solve.work: Smallest s, middle s+20, largest 3s. 5s+20 = 180, s = 32. Angles 32, 52, 96 (sum 180). Middle 52.

questions.skill: Angle sum with algebra or ratios
questions.stem: An isosceles triangle has two equal base angles of $(2x+5)^\circ$ each and a top angle of $(x+10)^\circ$. What is the measure of the top angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: $2(2x+5)+(x+10)=5x+20=180$, so $5x=160$ and $x=32$. The top angle is $32+10=42$ degrees. (The base angles are $69^\circ$ each.)

questions.skill: Which angle measures can form a triangle
questions.stem: Two angles of a triangle measure $100^\circ$ and $x^\circ$, where $x$ is a whole number. Which of these can NOT be the value of $x$?
questions.solution: The third angle is $180 - 100 - x = 80 - x$, and it must be more than 0. So $x$ must be less than 80. If $x = 80$ the third angle would be $0^\circ$. The values 20, 40 and 79 leave a third angle of 60, 40 and 1 degrees.

solve.work: Third angle = 80 - x must be > 0, so x < 80. 20, 40, 79 work (third 60, 40, 1). x = 80 leaves 0: cannot.

questions.skill: Which angle measures can form a triangle
questions.stem: Two angles of a triangle are each less than $40^\circ$, and all three angles are whole numbers of degrees. What is the smallest possible measure of the third angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: Each of the two angles is at most 39 degrees, so together they are at most $39 + 39 = 78$. The third angle is at least $180 - 78 = 102$ degrees.

solve.work: Two whole-number angles each less than 40 are at most 39 each, total at most 78. Third angle at least 180 - 78 = 102 (39, 39, 102).

questions.skill: How many triangles fit the given measures
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, angle $A$ is $110^\circ$, side $AB$ is 8 cm and side $BC$ is 5 cm. (Side $BC$ is the side opposite angle $A$.) How many different triangles fit this description?
questions.solution: The longest side of a triangle is opposite its largest angle. With an obtuse angle at $A$, side $BC$ would have to be the longest side, but $5 < 8$. If you try to swing a 5 cm side from $B$, it cannot reach the other arm of the $110^\circ$ angle. So there are 0 triangles.

solve.work: Angle A = 110 is obtuse, so the side opposite it (BC) must be the longest side. But BC = 5 < AB = 8. No triangle: 0.

questions.skill: How many triangles fit the given measures
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, angle $A$ is $30^\circ$, side $AB$ is 10 cm and side $BC$ is 6 cm. The shortest distance from point $B$ to the line that contains side $AC$ is 5 cm. How many different triangles fit this description?
questions.solution: Swing a 6 cm side from $B$. It is longer than the 5 cm shortest distance, so it reaches the line in two places, one on each side of the foot of the perpendicular. The foot is about 8.7 cm from $A$ and each point is about 3.3 cm from the foot, so both points lie on the ray from $A$ (about 5.4 cm and 12.0 cm from $A$). Two different triangles fit.

solve.work: C lies on the ray from A at 30 degrees to AB, and BC = 6. The distance from B to that line is 5 (= 10 x 1/2). Since 5 < 6, the circle of radius 6 about B meets the line at two points; since 6 < AB = 10, A is outside that circle, so both points lie on the same side of A (foot at 10cos30 = 8.66 from A, crossings at 8.66 +/- sqrt(11) = 5.34 and 11.98, both positive). Two triangles.

questions.skill: How many triangles fit the given measures
questions.stem: Which information could give MORE than one triangle?
choices: Sides of 6 cm, 7 cm and 9 cm
Sides of 6 cm and 9 cm, and the $40^\circ$ angle between them
Angles of $40^\circ$ and $60^\circ$, and the 9 cm side between them
Sides of 9 cm and 7 cm, and a $40^\circ$ angle opposite the 7 cm side
questions.answer: Sides of 9 cm and 7 cm, and a $40^\circ$ angle opposite the 7 cm side
questions.solution: Three sides, two sides with the angle between them, and two angles with the side between them each fix exactly one triangle. Two sides and an angle NOT between them can fit two triangles: the 7 cm side can swing to two places on the other arm of the $40^\circ$ angle.

solve.answer: Sides of 9 cm and 7 cm, and a $40^\circ$ angle opposite the 7 cm side
solve.work: SSS, ASA and SAS each fix one triangle. 9 and 7 with 40 degrees opposite 7 (SSA): the height from the vertex is 9 sin 40 = 5.79 < 7 < 9, so two triangles are possible. This option can give more than one.

questions.skill: How many triangles fit the given measures
questions.stem: A triangle has angles of $55^\circ$, $65^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. One of its sides is 10 cm long, but it is not said which one. Triangles with the same size and shape count as one. How many different triangles fit?
questions.solution: The 10 cm side could be opposite the $55^\circ$ angle, opposite the $65^\circ$ angle, or opposite the $60^\circ$ angle. Each choice gives a triangle of a different size. So there are 3 different triangles.

solve.work: All three angles differ, so all three sides differ. The 10 cm side can be opposite 55, 60 or 65, giving three different-sized triangles. 3.

questions.skill: How many triangles fit the given measures
questions.stem: A triangle has angles of $40^\circ$, $70^\circ$ and $70^\circ$. One of its sides is 6 cm long, but it is not said which one. Triangles with the same size and shape count as one. How many different triangles fit?
questions.solution: The 6 cm side could be opposite the $40^\circ$ angle, or opposite one of the $70^\circ$ angles. The two $70^\circ$ angles are alike, so putting the 6 cm side opposite either one gives the same triangle. That is 2 different triangles.

solve.work: Isosceles: the two sides opposite the 70 angles are equal. The 6 cm side is either the base (opposite 40) or one of the equal sides (opposite 70). Two different triangles.

questions.skill: Reason with a model, a rule or a claim
questions.stem: A triangle has one obtuse angle of $130^\circ$. All three angles are whole numbers of degrees. What is the greatest possible measure of the largest of the other two angles, in degrees?
questions.solution: The other two angles add to $180 - 130 = 50$ degrees, and each is at least 1 degree. The larger one is greatest when the smaller is 1: $50 - 1 = 49$ degrees.

solve.work: Other two angles sum to 180 - 130 = 50, each a whole number at least 1. Largest of them at most 49 (49 and 1).

questions.skill: Reason with a model, a rule or a claim
questions.stem: Ivy says, "Two triangles with the same three angles must be exactly the same triangle." Which pair shows that Ivy is wrong?
choices: Triangle P has sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm. Triangle Q has sides 4 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm
Triangle P has sides 5 cm, 5 cm, 5 cm. Triangle Q has sides 5 cm, 5 cm, 5 cm
Triangle P has sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm. Triangle Q has sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 6 cm
Triangle P has sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm. Triangle Q is P made twice as big, with sides 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm
questions.answer: Triangle P has sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm. Triangle Q is P made twice as big, with sides 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm
questions.solution: A counterexample needs two triangles with the same angles that are NOT the same size and shape. Making a triangle twice as big keeps every angle but changes the size. The pairs with matching sides are the same triangle, and sides 3, 4, 6 give different angles from 3, 4, 5.

solve.answer: Triangle P has sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm. Triangle Q is P made twice as big, with sides 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm
solve.work: 3,4,5 and 6,8,10 are similar (same angles) but different sizes, so they are not the same triangle. 3,4,5 vs 4,3,5 are the same triangle; equal equilaterals are the same; 3,4,6 has different angles.

questions.skill: Reason with a model, a rule or a claim
questions.stem: Why is it enough to check only that the two shortest sides add up to more than the longest side?
choices: The other two sums each include the longest side, so they are certain to be larger than the remaining side
The other two sums always come out equal to the first sum
The shortest side is always longer than half of the longest side
Only the longest side matters, so the others can be any length
questions.answer: The other two sums each include the longest side, so they are certain to be larger than the remaining side
questions.solution: The other two checks add the longest side to one of the others, and compare with the third side, which is no longer than the longest. So those sums are certain to be bigger. Only the first check can fail.

solve.answer: The other two sums each include the longest side, so they are certain to be larger than the remaining side
solve.work: With a <= b <= c: a + c > b and b + c > a hold automatically because c alone is at least as long as either other side and the added side is positive. Only a + b > c needs checking.

questions.skill: Reason with a model, a rule or a claim
questions.stem: A 12 cm piece of wire is cut into three pieces, each a whole number of centimeters long, and the pieces are used as the three sides of a triangle. Triangles with the same three side lengths count as one. How many different triangles can be made?
questions.solution: The longest piece must be less than half of 12, so it is at most 5. The sets of three whole numbers adding to 12 with longest at most 5 are 4, 4, 4; 3, 4, 5; and 2, 5, 5. Each satisfies the side rule ($2 + 5 = 7 > 5$). So 3 triangles can be made.

solve.work: a <= b <= c, a+b+c = 12, a+b > c so c < 6, and c >= 4. c=4: 4,4,4. c=5: a+b=7 with b<=5: 2,5,5 and 3,4,5. Three triangles.

questions.skill: Reason with a model, a rule or a claim
questions.stem: Which statement is true for every triangle?
choices: The longest side is longer than half of the perimeter
The longest side is shorter than half of the perimeter
The shortest side is longer than one third of the perimeter
The two shorter sides together are shorter than the longest side
questions.answer: The longest side is shorter than half of the perimeter
questions.solution: The longest side is less than the sum of the other two, so twice the longest side is less than the whole perimeter. That means the longest side is less than half the perimeter. For sides 3, 4, 5 the shortest side (3) is less than one third of 12 (which is 4).

solve.answer: The longest side is shorter than half of the perimeter
solve.work: Longest c < a + b, so 2c < a+b+c = P, c < P/2: always true. Longest > P/2 is false; shortest <= P/3 always, so the one-third statement is false; shorter two sum to more, not less.

questions.skill: Angle sum of a triangle
questions.stem: Two angles of a triangle measure $48^\circ$ and $67^\circ$. What is the measure of the third angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The three angles of a triangle add up to $180^\circ$. First, $48 + 67 = 115$. Then $180 - 115 = 65$.

questions.skill: Corresponding angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Angle 1 and angle 2 are corresponding angles. Angle 1 measures $110^\circ$. What is the measure of angle 2, in degrees?
questions.solution: When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, corresponding angles are equal. So angle 2 also measures $110^\circ$.

solve.work: Corresponding angles formed by parallel lines and a transversal are congruent, so angle 2 = 110.

questions.skill: Exterior angle of a triangle
questions.stem: One side of a triangle is extended to form an exterior angle. The two interior angles that are not next to the exterior angle measure $40^\circ$ and $55^\circ$. What is the measure of the exterior angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it. $40 + 55 = 95$. Check: the third interior angle is $180 - 95 = 85$, and $40 + 55 + 85 = 180$.

solve.work: Exterior angle = sum of the two remote interior angles = 40 + 55 = 95.

questions.skill: Angle sum of a triangle
questions.stem: Triangle $PQR$ has angle $P = 72^\circ$ and angle $Q = 38^\circ$. What is the measure of angle $R$, in degrees?
questions.solution: The angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$. $72 + 38 = 110$, and $180 - 110 = 70$. The number 110 is only the sum of the two angles, 108 is $180 - 72$, and 142 is $180 - 38$.

questions.skill: Angle sum of a triangle
questions.stem: Two angles of a triangle measure $25^\circ$ and $65^\circ$. What is the measure of the third angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: $25 + 65 = 90$, and $180 - 90 = 90$. So the third angle is a right angle. The number 40 is $65 - 25$, 115 is $180 - 65$, and 155 is $180 - 25$.

questions.skill: Angle sum of a triangle
questions.stem: In a right triangle, one of the acute angles is $28^\circ$. What is the measure of the other acute angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The right angle is $90^\circ$, so the two acute angles add to $180 - 90 = 90$ degrees. The other acute angle is $90 - 28 = 62$ degrees.

solve.work: Acute angles of a right triangle sum to 90: 90 - 28 = 62.

questions.skill: Angle sum of a triangle
questions.stem: An isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of $80^\circ$ between its two equal sides. What is the measure of each base angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The two base angles are equal and share $180 - 80 = 100$ degrees, so each is $100 \div 2 = 50$ degrees. The number 100 forgets to split the sum between the two angles.

questions.skill: Angle sum of a triangle with algebra
questions.stem: The angles of a triangle measure $x^\circ$, $(x+20)^\circ$ and $(x+40)^\circ$. What is the value of $x$?

questions.skill: Exterior angle from the two far interior angles
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, side $AC$ is extended past $C$ to a point $D$. Angle $A$ measures $35^\circ$ and angle $B$ measures $70^\circ$. What is the measure of the exterior angle $BCD$, in degrees?
questions.solution: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it. Angle $BCD$ is next to angle $C$, so $BCD = A + B = 35 + 70 = 105$ degrees.

solve.work: Exterior angle BCD = sum of the remote interior angles A + B = 35 + 70 = 105.

questions.skill: Exterior angle from the two far interior angles
questions.stem: A triangle has interior angles of $50^\circ$, $60^\circ$ and $70^\circ$. One side is extended to make an exterior angle at the vertex of the $70^\circ$ angle. What is the measure of that exterior angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it: $50 + 60 = 110$ degrees. (It also equals $180 - 70 = 110$.) The number 70 is the interior angle itself.

questions.skill: Exterior angle from the two far interior angles
questions.stem: Two interior angles of a triangle measure $40^\circ$ and $80^\circ$. What is the measure of the exterior angle at the third vertex, in degrees?
questions.solution: The exterior angle at the third vertex equals the sum of the other two interior angles: $40 + 80 = 120$ degrees.

solve.work: Exterior angle at third vertex = 40 + 80 = 120 (interior there is 60).

questions.skill: Interior angle from an exterior angle
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, the exterior angle at $C$ measures $110^\circ$ and angle $A$ measures $45^\circ$. What is the measure of angle $B$, in degrees?
questions.solution: The exterior angle at $C$ equals $A + B$. So $B = 110 - 45 = 65$ degrees.

solve.work: Exterior at C = A + B: 110 = 45 + B, B = 65.

questions.skill: Interior angle from an exterior angle
questions.stem: An exterior angle of a triangle measures $120^\circ$. What is the measure of the interior angle at the same vertex, in degrees?
questions.solution: The exterior angle and the interior angle at the same vertex make a straight line, so they add to $180^\circ$. The interior angle is $180 - 120 = 60$ degrees.

solve.work: Exterior and adjacent interior angles form a linear pair: 180 - 120 = 60.

questions.skill: Exterior angles with algebra
questions.stem: An exterior angle of a triangle measures $(2x+10)^\circ$. The two interior angles not next to it measure $50^\circ$ and $70^\circ$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two far interior angles: $2x + 10 = 50 + 70 = 120$. So $2x = 110$ and $x = 55$.

questions.skill: Linear pairs and vertical angles
questions.stem: Two lines cross. One of the four angles formed measures $65^\circ$. What is the measure of the angle directly opposite it, in degrees?
questions.solution: Angles directly opposite each other where two lines cross (vertical angles) are equal. So the answer is 65 degrees.

questions.skill: Linear pairs and vertical angles
questions.stem: Two angles form a linear pair. One of them measures $110^\circ$. What is the measure of the other, in degrees?
questions.solution: A linear pair makes a straight line, so the angles add to $180^\circ$. The other angle is $180 - 110 = 70$ degrees.

questions.skill: Linear pairs and vertical angles
questions.stem: Two lines cross, forming four angles. Which pair of these angles must be equal in measure?
choices: Two angles directly opposite each other
Two angles side by side on a straight line
Any two of the four angles
questions.answer: Two angles directly opposite each other
questions.solution: Angles directly opposite each other (vertical angles) are always equal. Two angles side by side on a line add to $180^\circ$ but are equal only when each is $90^\circ$.

solve.answer: Two angles directly opposite each other
solve.work: Vertical (opposite) angles are always equal. Adjacent angles add to 180 and are equal only if both are 90.

questions.skill: Linear pairs and vertical angles
questions.stem: Angle $A$ and angle $B$ are supplementary. Angle $A$ measures $125^\circ$. What is the measure of angle $B$, in degrees?
questions.solution: Supplementary angles add to $180^\circ$. So angle $B$ is $180 - 125 = 55$ degrees.

questions.skill: Corresponding angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Parallel lines $\ell$ and $m$ are crossed by a line $t$. Angle $a$ is at $\ell$ and angle $b$ is at $m$, and they are corresponding angles. Angle $a$ measures $75^\circ$. What is the measure of angle $b$, in degrees?
questions.solution: When parallel lines are crossed by a transversal, corresponding angles are equal. So angle $b$ measures 75 degrees.

solve.work: Corresponding angles on parallel lines are equal: 75.

questions.skill: Corresponding angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: A road crosses two parallel railroad tracks. At the first track, one of the angles formed measures $132^\circ$. What is the measure of the corresponding angle at the second track, in degrees?
questions.solution: The tracks are parallel, so corresponding angles are equal: 132 degrees. The number 48 is the angle next to it on a straight line ($180 - 132$).

questions.skill: Corresponding angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. Two corresponding angles measure $(x+30)^\circ$ and $80^\circ$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: Corresponding angles are equal, so $x + 30 = 80$ and $x = 50$.

questions.skill: Alternate interior and exterior angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Parallel lines $\ell$ and $m$ are crossed by a transversal. Angles $c$ and $d$ are alternate interior angles. Angle $c$ measures $58^\circ$. What is the measure of angle $d$, in degrees?
questions.solution: Alternate interior angles formed by parallel lines are equal. So angle $d$ measures 58 degrees.

solve.work: Alternate interior angles on parallel lines are equal: 58.

questions.skill: Alternate interior and exterior angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Two parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. Two alternate interior angles are formed, one at each line. One of them measures $105^\circ$. What is the measure of the other, in degrees?
questions.solution: Alternate interior angles formed by parallel lines are equal, so the other angle is also 105 degrees. The number 75 is the angle next to it on a straight line.

questions.skill: Alternate interior and exterior angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. Alternate exterior angles lie outside the parallel lines, on opposite sides of the transversal. One alternate exterior angle measures $120^\circ$. What is the measure of the other, in degrees?
questions.solution: Alternate exterior angles formed by parallel lines are equal. So the other angle measures 120 degrees.

solve.work: Alternate exterior angles on parallel lines are equal: 120.

questions.skill: Alternate interior and exterior angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. Two alternate interior angles measure $(x+20)^\circ$ and $55^\circ$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: Alternate interior angles are equal, so $x + 20 = 55$ and $x = 35$. The number 75 comes from adding 20 instead of subtracting.

questions.skill: Same-side interior angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. Two same-side interior angles are formed. One of them measures $70^\circ$. What is the measure of the other, in degrees?
questions.solution: Same-side interior angles formed by parallel lines add to $180^\circ$. The other angle is $180 - 70 = 110$ degrees.

questions.skill: Same-side interior angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Which pair of angles is NOT always equal in measure?
questions.answer: Same-side interior angles
questions.solution: Corresponding, alternate interior and alternate exterior angles are equal when the lines are parallel. Same-side interior angles add to $180^\circ$, so they are equal only when each is $90^\circ$.

solve.answer: Same-side interior angles
solve.work: Alternate interior, corresponding and alternate exterior angles are equal; same-side interior angles are supplementary, equal only when both are 90.

questions.skill: Choose the angle relationship from the positions
questions.stem: Parallel lines $\ell$ (the upper line) and $m$ (the lower line) are crossed by a transversal $t$. Angle $p$ is at $\ell$, above $\ell$ and to the left of $t$. Angle $q$ is at $m$, above $m$ and to the left of $t$. Angle $p$ measures $(2x+10)^\circ$ and angle $q$ measures $70^\circ$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: Angles $p$ and $q$ are in matching positions, so they are corresponding angles and are equal: $2x + 10 = 70$. Then $2x = 60$ and $x = 30$.

solve.work: Both above their line and left of t: corresponding angles, equal. 2x + 10 = 70, x = 30.

questions.skill: Choose the angle relationship from the positions
questions.stem: Parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. Two same-side interior angles measure $(3x)^\circ$ and $(x+40)^\circ$. Which equation can be used to find $x$?
questions.solution: Same-side interior angles formed by parallel lines are supplementary: they add to $180^\circ$. So $3x + (x+40) = 180$, which gives $x = 35$.

questions.skill: Tell whether lines are parallel from angle measures
questions.stem: Two lines are crossed by a transversal. A pair of corresponding angles each measure $65^\circ$. What can you conclude about the two lines?
choices: The two lines are not parallel
Nothing, because more angles are needed
questions.answer: The two lines are parallel
questions.solution: If corresponding angles are equal, the lines are parallel. This is the reverse of the rule for parallel lines. One equal pair of corresponding angles is enough.

solve.answer: The two lines are parallel
solve.work: Equal corresponding angles mean the lines are parallel (converse of the corresponding angles property).

questions.skill: Multi-step angle problems with parallel lines
questions.stem: A transversal crosses two parallel lines, forming eight angles. One of the eight angles measures $50^\circ$. How many of the other seven angles also measure $50^\circ$?
questions.solution: Four of the eight angles measure $50^\circ$ (the given one, its vertical angle, and the two corresponding angles at the other line). The other four measure $130^\circ$. So three of the other seven angles also measure 50 degrees.

solve.work: The eight angles are four of 50 and four of 130. Besides the given one, 3 others measure 50.

questions.skill: Multi-step angle problems in triangles and around points
questions.stem: Three angles fit together along a straight line. Two of them measure $35^\circ$ and $90^\circ$. What is the measure of the third angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: Angles along a straight line add to $180^\circ$. The third angle is $180 - 35 - 90 = 55$ degrees.

solve.work: Angles along a straight line sum to 180: 180 - 35 - 90 = 55.

questions.skill: Multi-step angle problems in triangles and around points
questions.stem: Four angles fit together around a point. Three of them measure $90^\circ$, $120^\circ$ and $75^\circ$. What is the measure of the fourth angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: Angles around a point add to $360^\circ$. $90 + 120 + 75 = 285$, and $360 - 285 = 75$ degrees. The number 285 is the sum of the three angles.

solve.work: Angles around a point sum to 360: 360 - 90 - 120 - 75 = 75.

questions.skill: Unknown angles in a triangle (algebra)
questions.stem: The angles of a triangle measure $(x+10)^\circ$, $(2x)^\circ$ and $(x+30)^\circ$. What is the measure of the largest angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The angles add up to $180$: $(x+10) + 2x + (x+30) = 4x + 40 = 180$, so $4x = 140$ and $x = 35$. The angles are $45^\circ$, $70^\circ$ and $65^\circ$. The largest is $70^\circ$.

questions.skill: Alternate interior angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Two alternate interior angles measure $(3x+5)^\circ$ and $65^\circ$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: Alternate interior angles are equal when the lines are parallel. So $3x + 5 = 65$. Subtract 5: $3x = 60$. Divide by 3: $x = 20$.

solve.work: Alternate interior angles are congruent: 3x + 5 = 65 -> 3x = 60 -> x = 20.

questions.skill: Same-side interior angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Two angles on the same side of the transversal and between the parallel lines measure $(2x+10)^\circ$ and $(x+20)^\circ$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: Same-side interior angles add up to $180^\circ$ when the lines are parallel. So $(2x+10) + (x+20) = 180$, which gives $3x + 30 = 180$. Then $3x = 150$ and $x = 50$. The angles are $110^\circ$ and $70^\circ$.

solve.work: Same-side interior angles are supplementary: (2x+10) + (x+20) = 180 -> 3x + 30 = 180 -> x = 50. Check: 110 + 70 = 180.

questions.skill: Angle sum of a triangle
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, angle $C$ measures $60^\circ$ and angle $A$ is twice as large as angle $B$. What is the measure of angle $A$, in degrees?
questions.solution: Angles $A$ and $B$ share $180 - 60 = 120$ degrees. Since $A$ is twice $B$, they are 3 equal parts: $B = 120 \div 3 = 40$ degrees and $A = 2 \times 40 = 80$ degrees.

questions.skill: Angle sum of a triangle with algebra
questions.stem: The angles of a triangle measure $(2x)^\circ$, $(3x)^\circ$ and $(4x)^\circ$. What is the measure of the smallest angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: $2x + 3x + 4x = 9x = 180$, so $x = 20$. The smallest angle is $2x = 40$ degrees. The number 20 is the value of $x$, and 60 and 80 are the other two angles.

questions.skill: Angle sum of a triangle with algebra
questions.stem: The angles of a triangle measure $(x+15)^\circ$, $(2x-5)^\circ$ and $(3x+2)^\circ$. What is the measure of the largest angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: $(x+15) + (2x-5) + (3x+2) = 6x + 12 = 180$, so $6x = 168$ and $x = 28$. The angles are $43^\circ$, $51^\circ$ and $86^\circ$, so the largest is 86 degrees.

questions.skill: Exterior angle from the two far interior angles
questions.stem: In triangle $PQR$, side $QR$ is extended past $R$ to a point $S$. Angle $P$ measures $58^\circ$ and angle $Q$ measures $47^\circ$. What is the measure of angle $PRS$, in degrees?
questions.solution: Angle $PRS$ is the exterior angle at $R$, so it equals $P + Q = 58 + 47 = 105$ degrees. The number 75 is the interior angle $R$ ($180 - 105$), 122 is $180 - 58$ and 133 is $180 - 47$.

solve.work: PRS is the exterior angle at R: P + Q = 58 + 47 = 105.

questions.skill: Exterior angle from the two far interior angles
questions.stem: A triangle has angles of $64^\circ$, $57^\circ$ and $59^\circ$. A side is extended to make an exterior angle at the vertex of the $59^\circ$ angle. What is the measure of that exterior angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it: $64 + 57 = 121$ degrees. Check: $180 - 59 = 121$.

questions.skill: Exterior angle from the two far interior angles
questions.stem: Which statement about an exterior angle of a triangle is always true?
choices: It is always an obtuse angle
It always equals the interior angle next to it
It is always smaller than each interior angle that is not next to it
It equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it
questions.answer: It equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it
questions.solution: The exterior angle and the interior angle next to it form a straight line, so the exterior angle is $180^\circ$ minus that interior angle, which equals the other two interior angles added together. It can be acute, it is not equal to its neighbour in general, and it is larger than each of the two far angles.

solve.answer: It equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it
solve.work: Exterior angle theorem: it equals the sum of the two remote interior angles. It is acute when the interior angle is obtuse, it is supplementary (not equal) to the adjacent interior angle, and it is larger than each remote angle.

questions.skill: Interior angle from an exterior angle
questions.stem: A triangle has an exterior angle of $140^\circ$. One of the two interior angles not next to it measures $90^\circ$. What is the measure of the other one, in degrees?
questions.solution: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it. So the other angle is $140 - 90 = 50$ degrees.

solve.work: Exterior = sum of the two remote interior angles: 140 - 90 = 50.

questions.skill: Interior angle from an exterior angle
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, the exterior angle at $A$ measures $100^\circ$ and angle $B$ measures $30^\circ$. What is the measure of angle $C$, in degrees?
questions.solution: The exterior angle at $A$ equals $B + C$, so $C = 100 - 30 = 70$ degrees. (Check: the interior angle at $A$ is $80^\circ$, and $80 + 30 + 70 = 180$.)

solve.work: Exterior at A = B + C: 100 = 30 + C, C = 70. Check: interior A = 80, 80+30+70 = 180.

questions.skill: Exterior angles with algebra
questions.stem: The exterior angle of a triangle measures $(3x+15)^\circ$. The two interior angles not next to it measure $(x+20)^\circ$ and $(x+45)^\circ$. What is the measure of the exterior angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: $3x + 15 = (x+20) + (x+45) = 2x + 65$, so $x = 50$. The exterior angle is $3 \times 50 + 15 = 165$ degrees. The number 50 is only $x$, and 70 is one of the far angles.

questions.skill: Linear pairs and vertical angles
questions.stem: Two lines cross. One angle measures $(3x)^\circ$ and the angle directly opposite it measures $(x+50)^\circ$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: Opposite angles are equal, so $3x = x + 50$. Then $2x = 50$ and $x = 25$. (The angle itself is $75^\circ$.)

questions.skill: Linear pairs and vertical angles
questions.stem: Two lines cross, forming four angles. One angle is 4 times as large as an angle next to it. What is the measure of the smaller of these two angles, in degrees?
questions.solution: Angles next to each other where two lines cross add to $180^\circ$. With parts of 1 and 4, that is 5 equal parts: $180 \div 5 = 36$ degrees. The larger angle is $4 \times 36 = 144$ degrees.

solve.work: Adjacent angles form a linear pair: x + 4x = 180, x = 36 (other 144). Smaller 36.

questions.skill: Corresponding angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Two parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. Two corresponding angles measure $(4x-15)^\circ$ and $(2x+25)^\circ$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: Corresponding angles are equal: $4x - 15 = 2x + 25$, so $2x = 40$ and $x = 20$. (Each angle is $65^\circ$.)

questions.skill: Corresponding angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. An angle of $64^\circ$ at the upper line has a corresponding angle at the lower line. Angle $z$ forms a linear pair with that corresponding angle. What is the measure of angle $z$, in degrees?
questions.solution: The corresponding angle at the lower line is also $64^\circ$. A linear pair adds to $180^\circ$, so angle $z$ is $180 - 64 = 116$ degrees.

solve.work: Corresponding angle at the lower line is 64; z forms a linear pair with it: 180 - 64 = 116.

questions.skill: Alternate interior and exterior angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. Two alternate interior angles measure $(2x+14)^\circ$ and $(4x-26)^\circ$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: Alternate interior angles are equal: $2x + 14 = 4x - 26$, so $2x = 40$ and $x = 20$. The number 32 would come from wrongly adding the angles to $180^\circ$.

questions.skill: Alternate interior and exterior angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. Two alternate exterior angles measure $(5x-8)^\circ$ and $(3x+16)^\circ$. What is the measure of each of these angles, in degrees?
questions.solution: Alternate exterior angles are equal: $5x - 8 = 3x + 16$, so $2x = 24$ and $x = 12$. Each angle is $5 \times 12 - 8 = 52$ degrees.

questions.skill: Same-side interior angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. Two same-side interior angles measure $(3x+10)^\circ$ and $(2x+20)^\circ$. What is the measure of the larger of the two angles, in degrees?
questions.solution: Same-side interior angles add to $180^\circ$: $(3x+10) + (2x+20) = 5x + 30 = 180$, so $x = 30$. The angles are $100^\circ$ and $80^\circ$, and the larger is 100. (If they were set equal, $x$ would be 10 and each angle 40: wrong.)

questions.skill: Same-side interior angles and parallel lines
questions.stem: Two same-side interior angles formed by parallel lines and a transversal differ by $20^\circ$. What is the measure of the smaller angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The two angles add to $180^\circ$ and differ by 20. Taking 20 off the total leaves $160^\circ$ shared equally, so the smaller is $160 \div 2 = 80$ degrees and the larger is 100.

questions.solution: Both angles are between the parallel lines and on opposite sides of the transversal, so they are alternate interior angles and are equal: $3x - 5 = x + 35$, so $x = 20$. Angle $p$ is $3 \times 20 - 5 = 55$ degrees.

solve.work: p is below l (interior) left of t; q is above m (interior) right of t: alternate interior angles, equal. 3x - 5 = x + 35, x = 20. p = 55.

questions.skill: Tell whether lines are parallel from angle measures
questions.stem: Lines $a$ and $b$ are crossed by a transversal. Which pair of angle measures shows that $a$ and $b$ are parallel?
questions.answer: Alternate interior angles of $70^\circ$ and $70^\circ$
questions.solution: Lines are parallel when alternate interior (or corresponding) angles are equal, or when same-side interior angles add to $180^\circ$. Only alternate interior angles of $70^\circ$ and $70^\circ$ meet one of these tests. Same-side angles of 70 and 70 add to 140.

solve.answer: Alternate interior angles of $70^\circ$ and $70^\circ$
solve.work: Equal alternate interior angles prove the lines parallel. Same-side interior 70 + 70 = 140 is not 180; corresponding 70 and 110 are unequal; alternate interior 70 and 110 are unequal.

questions.solution: Corresponding angles are equal, so angle 2 is $52^\circ$. Angle 3 forms a linear pair with angle 2, so it is $180 - 52 = 128$ degrees. The number 52 stops after the first step.

Both of these angles lie outside the triangle. What is the measure of angle $BAC$, in degrees?
questions.solution: The two outside angles and angle $BAC$ fit together along the straight line through $A$, so they add to $180^\circ$. Angle $BAC$ is $180 - 48 - 65 = 67$ degrees. (Check: by alternate interior angles, $B = 48^\circ$ and $C = 65^\circ$, and $48 + 65 + 67 = 180$.) The number 113 is only $48 + 65$.

solve.work: Exterior at A = B + C = 140, B = C, so B = 70 (interior A = 40).

solve.work: Exterior at an acute vertex = sum of the remote angles = 90 + other acute angle: 115 - 90 = 25. (Interior there is 65; 65 + 25 = 90.)

questions.skill: Exterior angle with algebra
questions.stem: A triangle has an exterior angle that measures $(4x-10)^\circ$. The two interior angles that are not next to it measure $(x+20)^\circ$ and $(x+30)^\circ$. What is the measure of the exterior angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two far interior angles: $4x - 10 = (x+20) + (x+30) = 2x + 50$. So $2x = 60$ and $x = 30$. The exterior angle is $4(30) - 10 = 110^\circ$. Check: $50 + 60 = 110$.

solve.work: Exterior angle = sum of remote interiors: 4x - 10 = (x+20) + (x+30) = 2x + 50 -> 2x = 60 -> x = 30. Exterior = 4(30) - 10 = 110 (remote interiors 50 and 60).

questions.solution: Corresponding angles are equal, so $5x - 12 = 3x + 18$. Then $2x = 30$ and $x = 15$. The angle is $5(15) - 12 = 63^\circ$. A linear pair adds up to $180^\circ$, so the other angle is $180 - 63 = 117^\circ$.

solve.work: Corresponding angles equal: 5x - 12 = 3x + 18 -> 2x = 30 -> x = 15. Angle = 5(15) - 12 = 63. Linear pair: 180 - 63 = 117.

questions.skill: Multi-step angle problems with parallel lines
questions.stem: Triangle $ABC$ has side $BC$ extended past $C$ to a point $D$. Ray $CE$ starts at $C$, is parallel to side $AB$, and lies on the same side of line $BD$ as point $A$. Angle $ACE$ measures $40^\circ$ and angle $ECD$ measures $55^\circ$. What is the measure of angle $ACB$, in degrees?
questions.solution: Angle $ACD = ACE + ECD = 40 + 55 = 95$ degrees. Angle $ACB$ and angle $ACD$ form a linear pair, so $ACB = 180 - 95 = 85$ degrees. (Check: $A = 40^\circ$ and $B = 55^\circ$ by parallel lines, and $40 + 55 + 85 = 180$.)

solve.work: CE parallel to AB: ECD = B = 55 (corresponding, transversal BD) and ACE = A = 40 (alternate interior, transversal AC). Exterior ACD = 40 + 55 = 95, so ACB = 180 - 95 = 85.

questions.skill: Multi-step angle problems with parallel lines
questions.stem: A transversal crosses two parallel lines, forming eight angles. One angle measures $(2x+10)^\circ$ and another angle measures $(3x-20)^\circ$. The two angles are NOT equal. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: Any two of the eight angles are either equal or add to $180^\circ$. Since these two are not equal, they add to $180^\circ$: $(2x+10) + (3x-20) = 5x - 10 = 180$, so $5x = 190$ and $x = 38$. (The angles are $86^\circ$ and $94^\circ$.)

solve.work: With parallel lines, any two of the eight angles are either equal or supplementary. Not equal, so (2x+10) + (3x-20) = 180, 5x = 190, x = 38. Angles 86 and 94, indeed unequal.

questions.skill: Multi-step angle problems in triangles and around points
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, angle $A$ measures $76^\circ$ and angle $B$ measures $54^\circ$. Point $D$ is on side $BC$ and $AD$ bisects angle $A$. What is the measure of angle $ADC$, in degrees?
questions.solution: Angle $BAD$ is half of $76^\circ$, which is $38^\circ$. Angle $ADC$ is an exterior angle of triangle $ABD$, so it equals $B + BAD = 54 + 38 = 92$ degrees. (Check: angle $C = 50^\circ$, and in triangle $ADC$: $38 + 92 + 50 = 180$.)

solve.work: BAD = 76/2 = 38. ADC is the exterior angle of triangle ABD at D: 38 + 54 = 92. Check: C = 50, triangle ADC: 38 + 50 + 92 = 180.

questions.skill: Multi-step angle problems in triangles and around points
questions.stem: A triangle has one exterior angle drawn at each vertex. What is the sum of these three exterior angles, in degrees?
questions.solution: Each exterior angle is $180^\circ$ minus its interior angle. The three together are $3 \times 180 - 180 = 360$ degrees, because the three interior angles add to $180^\circ$.

questions.skill: Multi-step angle problems in triangles and around points
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, angle $B$ measures $50^\circ$ and angle $C$ measures $70^\circ$. The bisectors of angles $B$ and $C$ meet at point $I$ inside the triangle. What is the measure of angle $BIC$, in degrees?
questions.solution: Half of angle $B$ is $25^\circ$ and half of angle $C$ is $35^\circ$. In triangle $BIC$, angle $BIC = 180 - 25 - 35 = 120$ degrees.

questions.skill: Multi-step angle problems in triangles and around points
questions.stem: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio $2:3:4$. What is the measure of the largest exterior angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: There are $2 + 3 + 4 = 9$ parts, so one part is $20^\circ$. The interior angles are $40^\circ$, $60^\circ$ and $80^\circ$. Each exterior angle is $180^\circ$ minus its interior angle: 140, 120 and 100 degrees. The largest is 140.

solve.work: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 parts = 180, 20 each: angles 40, 60, 80. Largest exterior is at the smallest angle: 180 - 40 = 140.

questions.skill: Multi-step angle problems in triangles and around points
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, point $D$ is on side $BC$. Angle $BAD$ measures $30^\circ$, angle $ADC$ measures $100^\circ$ and angle $C$ measures $45^\circ$. What is the measure of angle $BAC$, in degrees?
questions.solution: In triangle $ADC$, angle $DAC = 180 - 100 - 45 = 35$ degrees. Angle $BAC = BAD + DAC = 30 + 35 = 65$ degrees.

questions.solution: The Pythagorean Theorem says that the sum of the squares of the two legs equals the square of the hypotenuse: $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

solve.work: Pythagorean Theorem with legs a, b and hypotenuse c: a^2 + b^2 = c^2.

questions.skill: Find a leg of a right triangle in context
questions.stem: A 20-foot ladder leans against a wall. The bottom of the ladder is 16 feet from the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach, in feet?
questions.solution: The ladder is the hypotenuse of a right triangle. $16^2 + h^2 = 20^2$, so $h^2 = 400 - 256 = 144$ and $h = 12$ feet.

questions.skill: Choose or write the Pythagorean equation
questions.stem: In a right triangle, which side is called the hypotenuse?
choices: The side opposite the right angle
The shortest side of the triangle
Either side that touches the right angle
The side the triangle rests on
questions.answer: The side opposite the right angle
questions.solution: The hypotenuse is the side across from the right angle. It is also the longest side of a right triangle. The two sides that touch the right angle are the legs.

solve.answer: The side opposite the right angle
solve.work: The hypotenuse is by definition the side opposite the right angle (also the longest side).

questions.skill: Choose or write the Pythagorean equation
questions.stem: In right triangle $XYZ$, the right angle is at $Y$. Which equation is true?
questions.solution: The right angle is at $Y$, so the hypotenuse is the side across from $Y$, which is $XZ$. The squares of the two legs add to the square of the hypotenuse: $XY^2 + YZ^2 = XZ^2$.

solve.work: Right angle at Y, so the legs are XY and YZ and the hypotenuse is XZ (opposite Y). XY^2 + YZ^2 = XZ^2.

questions.skill: Choose or write the Pythagorean equation
questions.stem: A right triangle has side lengths 9 cm, 40 cm and 41 cm. Which length is the hypotenuse?
questions.answer: 41 cm
questions.solution: The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle. Here that is 41 cm. (Check: $9^2 + 40^2 = 81 + 1600 = 1681 = 41^2$.)

solve.answer: 41 cm
solve.work: Hypotenuse is the longest side: 41 cm. Check 81 + 1600 = 1681 = 41^2.

questions.solution: The Pythagorean Theorem says the areas of the squares on the two legs add up to the area of the square on the hypotenuse. $9 + 16 = 25$ square centimeters.

solve.work: Area on hypotenuse = sum of areas on legs = 9 + 16 = 25.

questions.skill: Verify the theorem and squares on the sides

questions.solution: The area of the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the areas of the squares on the legs: $25 + 144 = 169$ square yards.

solve.work: Square on longest side (hypotenuse) = 25 + 144 = 169 sq yd.

questions.skill: Verify the theorem and squares on the sides

questions.solution: The two shorter sides are the legs and 10 is the hypotenuse. $6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10^2$, so the equation $6^2 + 8^2 = 10^2$ is true. The other equations are false.

solve.work: 36 + 64 = 100, i.e. 6^2 + 8^2 = 10^2 (legs squared sum to hypotenuse squared).

questions.stem: On a coordinate plane, point $A$ is at $(0, 0)$ and point $B$ is at $(6, 8)$. What is the distance from $A$ to $B$, in units?
questions.solution: Go 6 units across and 8 units up to form a right triangle with legs 6 and 8. $6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100$, so the distance is $\sqrt{100} = 10$ units.

questions.skill: Distance on the coordinate plane
questions.stem: A right triangle on a coordinate plane has corners at $(1, 1)$, $(4, 1)$ and $(4, 5)$. How long is the side from $(1, 1)$ to $(4, 5)$, in units?
questions.solution: The legs run from $(1, 1)$ to $(4, 1)$, which is 3 units, and from $(4, 1)$ to $(4, 5)$, which is 4 units. The side asked about is the hypotenuse: $3^2 + 4^2 = 25$, so its length is 5 units.

questions.solution: The legs of the right triangle are 5 and 12, and the distance $d$ is the hypotenuse. So $d^2 = 5^2 + 12^2$.

questions.solution: The width, height and diagonal form a right triangle. $12^2 + 9^2 = 144 + 81 = 225$, and $\sqrt{225} = 15$ inches.

solve.work: Rise and run perpendicular: s^2 = 25 + 144 = 169, s = 13.

questions.skill: Pythagorean Theorem in a real-world problem

questions.skill: Pythagorean Theorem in a real-world problem

questions.solution: The tree height and the distance to the stake are the legs, and the rope ladder is the hypotenuse. $15^2 + 8^2 = 225 + 64 = 289$, and $\sqrt{289} = 17$ feet.

solve.issues: The 8 ft is measured from the tree's base, but the ladder starts at the floor's edge, which is not over the trunk; strictly the horizontal leg is unknown. Better: 'a stake 8 feet from the point directly below the edge of the floor'.

questions.solution: The other leg is $\sqrt{13^2 - 12^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ cm. The two legs are the base and the height, so the area is $\frac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 5 = 30$ square centimeters.

questions.skill: Converse of the Pythagorean Theorem

It is not a right triangle, because $8+15\ne 17$
It is not a right triangle, because $8^2+17^2\ne 15^2$

questions.answer: It is a right triangle, because $8^2+15^2=17^2$
questions.solution: Test the converse with the longest side as the hypotenuse: $8^2 + 15^2 = 64 + 225 = 289$ and $17^2 = 289$. The two are equal, so the triangle is a right triangle.

solve.answer: It is a right triangle, because $8^2+15^2=17^2$

questions.solution: Start from $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ and subtract $a^2$ from both sides: $b^2 = c^2 - a^2$.

questions.skill: Choose or write the Pythagorean equation

questions.solution: The ladder is the hypotenuse (17 feet). The wall height $h$ and the distance 8 feet are the legs. So $h^2 + 8^2 = 17^2$.

solve.work: Wall height h and base 8 are legs, ladder 17 is hypotenuse: h^2 + 8^2 = 17^2 (h = 15).

questions.skill: Choose or write the Pythagorean equation
questions.stem: Which statement is NOT true for every right triangle with legs $a$ and $b$ and hypotenuse $c$?
questions.answer: $a + b = c$
questions.solution: The squares add up, not the lengths: $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$. For example, the legs 3 and 4 give a hypotenuse of 5, and $3 + 4 = 7$, not 5. The other three statements are true for every right triangle.

solve.answer: $a + b = c$
solve.work: a^2+b^2=c^2, c longest, c^2-a^2=b^2 always true. a + b = c is never true (triangle inequality).

questions.skill: Distance on the coordinate plane
questions.stem: Which point is exactly 5 units from the origin $(0, 0)$?
questions.solution: The distance from the origin to $(x, y)$ is $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$. For $(3, 4)$ it is $\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$. The others give $\sqrt{34}$, $\sqrt{32}$ and $\sqrt{13}$.

questions.skill: Pythagorean Theorem in a real-world problem
questions.stem: An airplane is flying 12 kilometers above the ground. It is a horizontal distance of 35 kilometers from the airport. What is the straight-line distance from the plane to the airport, in kilometers?
questions.solution: The height and the horizontal distance are the legs of a right triangle. $12^2 + 35^2 = 144 + 1225 = 1369$, and $\sqrt{1369} = 37$ km.

questions.skill: Pythagorean Theorem in a real-world problem
questions.stem: A drone flies 24 meters due north and then 10 meters due west. How far is the drone, in a straight line, from where it started, in meters?
questions.solution: The two flights are the legs of a right triangle. $24^2 + 10^2 = 576 + 100 = 676$, and $\sqrt{676} = 26$ meters.

questions.skill: Pythagorean Theorem in a real-world problem
questions.stem: A rectangular gate frame is 3.6 m wide and 4.8 m tall. A brace runs along the diagonal between opposite corners. How long is the brace, in meters?

questions.skill: Multi-step problems with right triangles
questions.stem: Eli can walk along two sides of a rectangular park, 60 meters and then 80 meters, or he can take the straight diagonal path across the park. How many meters shorter is the diagonal path?
questions.solution: The diagonal is the hypotenuse: $60^2 + 80^2 = 3600 + 6400 = 10000$, so it is 100 m. Walking the two sides is $60 + 80 = 140$ m. The diagonal saves $140 - 100 = 40$ meters.

solve.work: Diagonal sqrt(3600 + 6400) = 100. Along sides 140. 140 - 100 = 40 m shorter.

questions.skill: Multi-step problems with right triangles
questions.stem: The diagonal of a rectangle is 17 cm and one side is 15 cm. What is the perimeter of the rectangle, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The other side is $\sqrt{17^2 - 15^2} = \sqrt{289 - 225} = \sqrt{64} = 8$ cm. The perimeter is $2 \times (15 + 8) = 46$ cm.

questions.skill: Multi-step problems with right triangles
questions.stem: A rectangle has a diagonal of 26 cm and a width of 10 cm. What is the area of the rectangle, in square centimeters?
questions.solution: The length is $\sqrt{26^2 - 10^2} = \sqrt{676 - 100} = \sqrt{576} = 24$ cm. The area is $10 \times 24 = 240$ square centimeters.

questions.skill: Distance between points with negative coordinates
questions.stem: Point $A$ is at $(-5, -2)$ and point $B$ is at $(2, 22)$ on a coordinate plane. What is the distance from $A$ to $B$, in units?
questions.solution: The horizontal change is $2 - (-5) = 7$ and the vertical change is $22 - (-2) = 24$. The distance is $\sqrt{7^2 + 24^2} = \sqrt{49 + 576} = \sqrt{625} = 25$.

questions.skill: Distance on the coordinate plane (square root answer)
questions.stem: Point $P$ is at $(-2, 5)$ and point $Q$ is at $(3, -1)$ on a coordinate plane. What is the distance from $P$ to $Q$, in units?
questions.solution: The horizontal change is $3 - (-2) = 5$ and the vertical change is $5 - (-1) = 6$. The distance is $\sqrt{5^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{25 + 36} = \sqrt{61}$.

questions.skill: Pythagorean Theorem in an isosceles triangle
questions.stem: An isosceles triangle has two sides that are each 17 cm long and a base that is 16 cm long. What is the height of the triangle from the base to the opposite corner, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The height cuts the base into two halves of 8 cm and makes a right triangle with hypotenuse 17 cm. So $h^2 + 8^2 = 17^2$, which gives $h^2 = 289 - 64 = 225$ and $h = 15$ cm.

solve.work: The height bisects the base: half-base 8, side 17. h = sqrt(17^2 - 8^2) = sqrt(289 - 64) = sqrt(225) = 15.

questions.skill: Choose or write the Pythagorean equation
questions.stem: The legs of a right triangle are $x$ and $x + 1$, and its hypotenuse is 5. Which equation is true?
questions.solution: The sum of the squares of the two legs equals the square of the hypotenuse: $x^2 + (x + 1)^2 = 5^2$. Be careful to square the whole quantity $x + 1$ and to square the 5 as well.

solve.work: Sum of squares of legs equals square of hypotenuse: x^2 + (x+1)^2 = 5^2 (x = 3).

questions.skill: Choose or write the Pythagorean equation
questions.stem: Each leg of a right triangle is made 3 times as long. What happens to the length of the hypotenuse?
questions.answer: It is also multiplied by 3
questions.solution: If the legs are $3a$ and $3b$, the hypotenuse squared is $9a^2 + 9b^2 = 9c^2$, so the new hypotenuse is $\sqrt{9c^2} = 3c$. For example, a 3-4-5 triangle becomes a 9-12-15 triangle.

solve.answer: It is also multiplied by 3

questions.skill: Verify the theorem and squares on the sides
